From rugby criticism to resilience: Former Fijiana Mere Moto shares her journey on fijivillage Her-Story at 7pm tonight
item.description: From facing criticism for playing rugby to overcoming the loss of her parents and best friend, Suva Women’s Rugby Strength and Conditioning Coach Mere Moto shares her powerful journey on fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono tonight at 7pm. Moto is also a former Fijiana XV and Fijian Drua Women Strength and Conditioning Coach, as well as a former Fijiana XV player.
item.content:encoded:
From facing criticism for playing rugby to overcoming the loss of her parents and best friend, Suva Women’s Rugby Strength and Conditioning Coach Mere Moto shares her powerful journey on fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono tonight at 7pm.

Moto is also a former Fijiana XV and Fijian Drua Women Strength and Conditioning Coach, as well as a former Fijiana XV player.

She made her debut against Papua New Guinea 10 years ago at the then ANZ Stadium, and a decade later, she received her official Test cap at the same venue, now HFC Bank Stadium, during the Fijiana XV’s first Test against South Africa this month.

Tonight, she opens up about her rugby journey, personal losses and finding the strength to move forward.

She will also demonstrate basic strength and conditioning techniques.

You can watch fijivillage Her-Story at 7pm tonight at 7pm on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and X, fijivillage.

You can also catch the podcast, fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono, on Spotify and Apple Podcasts.

item.title: Children may be carrying an ‘invisible bag’ of hurt and pain to school every day – Naisele
item.description: Parents are being urged to look beyond their children’s school results and behaviour and understand the emotional struggles they may be carrying every day. This was one of the key messages from Substance Abuse Advisory Council Director Josua Naisele while speaking at the Methodist Women’s Conference at the World Harvest Centre.
item.content:encoded:
Parents are being urged to look beyond their children’s school results and behaviour and understand the emotional struggles they may be carrying every day.

This was one of the key messages from Substance Abuse Advisory Council Director Josua Naisele while speaking at the Methodist Women’s Conference at the World Harvest Centre.

Naisele says children are gifts from God, and parents need to be careful about the words they use when correcting their children, as negative words can shape how children see themselves.

He says parents sometimes measure a child’s intelligence by their position in class or whether they receive a prize, but intelligence can also be reflected in a child’s ability to learn skills, solve problems and use their individual talents.

Naisele says a child who learns how to cook, plant food or carry out other practical tasks is also showing intelligence.

He says parents should recognise the different abilities of their children and help them develop confidence in their talents rather than constantly comparing them with others.

Naisele also highlighted the importance of creating an emotionally safe home, saying children do not only grow up in a house but also in the emotional environment their families create.

He says children may have a good home, attend a good school and have everything they need materially but can still feel emotionally unsafe.

Naisele used the example of an “invisible bag” that some children carry to school every day, filled with trauma, hurt and pain from what they experience or hear at home.

He says children remember how they feel around their parents and should be able to look forward to returning home after school knowing they will be loved, respected and supported.

Naisele says words such as telling children they are stupid, useless, a problem or that their parents are ashamed of them can remain with children and eventually influence what they believe about themselves.

He says fear does not necessarily teach children better behaviour but can instead teach them to remain silent about what they are going through.

Naisele says some children may then turn to drugs or other harmful behaviour as a way of dealing with the pain and pressure they are carrying.

He says when a child makes a mistake, parents should address the behaviour rather than attack the child personally, while making it clear that they remain supported and that problems can be worked through together.

Naisele also stressed the need for routine, stability, respectful communication, encouragement, attention and support in the home.

He says guidance must begin at home because children will eventually enter environments where they face peer pressure, social influences and exposure to drugs, and they need to be prepared to make the right decisions.

Naisele also highlighted concerns about children being referred for counselling because of problems within their families, including parental separation and divorce.

He says another emerging concern involves parents leaving Fiji for employment opportunities overseas, with one or both parents leaving their children in Fiji.

Naisele says strong and supportive families remain important in protecting children and helping them deal with the challenges they face as they grow up.

item.title: Two more arrested over viral Nadi robbery
item.description: Two more suspects allegedly involved in the aggravated robbery of a taxi driver in Nadi yesterday morning, are now in Police custody. Police say the development follows the surrender of the first suspect yesterday, after a video of the alleged robbery went viral.
item.content:encoded:
Two more suspects allegedly involved in the aggravated robbery of a taxi driver in Nadi yesterday morning, are now in Police custody.

Police say the development follows the surrender of the first suspect yesterday, after a video of the alleged robbery went viral.

The Western Division Taskforce is continuing its search for a fourth suspect, whose identity is known to Police.

Investigations into the incident continue.

item.title: $18.5M in Govt M-PAiSA and MyCash accounts were used for Govt payments - PS Finance
item.description: This has been clarified by the Ministry of Finance with the Office of the Auditor-General during the audit exit meeting, but the Ministry says the explanation does not appear to have been appropriately reflected in the audit report. They say the funds have been used for payments including the inflation mitigation payout, bus fare subsidies and back-to-school support.
item.content:encoded:
This has been clarified by the Ministry of Finance with the Office of the Auditor-General during the audit exit meeting, but the Ministry says the explanation does not appear to have been appropriately reflected in the audit report.

They say the funds have been used for payments including the inflation mitigation payout, bus fare subsidies and back-to-school support.

Permanent Secretary for Finance Shiri Goundar says Digital payments through M-PAiSA and MyCash have become a key part of Government’s payment system, with almost $500 million disbursed through the platforms since 2020.

Goundar says the payments include COVID-19 unemployment assistance, inflation mitigation payments, bus fare subsidies and back-to-school support.

He says M-PAiSA and MyCash serve a similar purpose to Government bank accounts, where sufficient funds are maintained to meet payment needs.

Goundar says proper internal controls and reconciliation processes are in place to ensure taxpayer funds are used in accordance with appropriations approved by Parliament.

He adds records are maintained and available for reconciliation and audit verification, while a standard operating procedure is in place for the use and recording of digital wallet funds in Government accounts.

item.title: More than 300 student cases reported to Substance Abuse Advisory Council this year - Naisele
item.description: More than 300 cases involving students have been reported to the Substance Abuse Advisory Council so far this year, mostly involving bullying, disrespectful behaviour and other behavioural issues. Speaking to about 2,000 women during the Methodist Women’s Conference at the World Harvest Centre, Director of the Substance Abuse Advisory Council Josua Naisele says students are facing growing social c
item.content:encoded:
More than 300 cases involving students have been reported to the Substance Abuse Advisory Council so far this year, mostly involving bullying, disrespectful behaviour and other behavioural issues.

Speaking to about 2,000 women during the Methodist Women’s Conference at the World Harvest Centre, Director of the Substance Abuse Advisory Council Josua Naisele says students are facing growing social challenges , including bullying, peer pressure, social media, violence and, in some cases, drug use.

He is urging parents to better understand what their children are going through before judging them.

Naisele says there have also been a few cases they received involved drugs and cyberbullying.

He says many behavioural issues among students can be linked to peer pressure, curiosity, social media and the environments in which children grow up.

Naisele says peer pressure remains a major challenge, as some children may be influenced by friends who introduce them to behaviour that are not encouraged at home .

He says some students may also turn to drugs as a way of coping with problems, while curiosity can lead young people to experiment with smoking and other harmful behaviour.

Naisele says children can also be influenced by what they see around them, including violence and drug use in their homes and communities.

He says social media and access to the internet have added another challenge, with young people being exposed to content that may not be suitable for them.

Naisele is urging parents to build stronger connections with their children through communication, understanding and positive support.

He says simply living under the same roof does not necessarily mean parents and children are connected .

Naisele says parents should create a home environment where children feel respected and supported and are comfortable enough to talk about the problems they are facing.

He is also urging parents not to immediately judge their children when they open up about their problems, as this can affect them emotionally and make it more difficult for them to seek help.

Naisele says students should not be afraid to seek counselling, stressing that counselling is about supporting them rather than judging them.

He says counsellors listen to students and guide them towards the support they need, while cases involving drugs, cyberbullying and other serious matters are referred to the relevant authorities.

Naisele says the Methodist Women’s Conference is an important platform, as the women will return to their churches, villages and communities across Fiji and Rotuma with the knowledge shared during the conference.

He says the women were encouraged to first apply what they have learned in their own lives and families before sharing the message with others.

Naisele says stronger communication, awareness and understanding within families can help provide students with the support they need to deal with the challenges they face in their daily lives.
